Chapter Two: The Case for Something Beyond Nature
Picture yourself walking through a quiet forest. You notice how sunlight filters through the leaves, and how the trees reach up toward the sky. Sure, science can tell us how these trees grow, how the sun moves, and even what’s happening in the soil beneath your feet.
But when it comes to that deep sense of right and wrong—well, science doesn't quite have the tools for that. The moral law isn’t something you can hold or see, but it feels just as real as the ground you’re standing on.
Now, some folks say this moral sense is just something we picked up through evolution or from the society around us. They argue that it’s an instinct, hardwired because it helped our ancestors survive. That’s one way to look at it. But think of instincts like the keys on a piano—they’re important, but they’re not the whole song. The moral law? That’s more like the sheet music, telling us which notes to play and when.
Imagine a moment when you feel torn between helping someone and looking out for yourself. Two instincts, pulling in different directions. The moral law helps you sort out which one to follow. It’s not just a gut feeling—it’s a guide.
Then there’s the idea that morality is just about what we like or don’t like, kind of like picking your favorite ice cream flavor. But think about the way we talk about fairness. When someone says, “That’s not fair,” they’re not just sharing a personal taste—they’re reaching for a standard they expect everyone else to recognize. It’s not about preference. It’s about what’s owed.
If you look at the universe as nothing more than atoms and forces, you end up with a pretty bleak picture. In that kind of world, moral obligations don’t really fit. Right and wrong would just be useful tricks—nothing more. But honestly, most of us can’t live that way. That sense of duty, that feeling of guilt, that longing for justice—they stick with us. They’re just too real to brush aside.
So, here’s where things get interesting. Are we supposed to believe that the moral law is just a weird accident? Or could it be pointing to something more, something beyond what we can touch or see? Maybe there’s a mind behind the universe—a source of meaning and purpose. Not just a force or a set of rules, but something personal. Something that actually cares about right and wrong.
Of course, some people push back against this idea. They worry it’ll lead to superstition or rigid beliefs. But if we’re really after the truth, we’ve got to be willing to follow the evidence—even if it takes us somewhere unexpected. The moral law isn’t a proof like two plus two equals four. But it’s a pretty strong signpost, pointing us toward something greater. It invites us to look deeper, to consider that maybe the universe isn’t just a giant machine, but a story—one with real meaning.
And honestly, this is just the start of the journey. Recognizing the moral law and its source is only the first step. The real question now is, what does all this mean for you and me, in our everyday lives? How does it affect the choices we make? What kind of person do we want to become?
At the end of the day, it’s not just about what’s true—it’s about what’s good, and how we choose to live in the light of it.
